title: Factorising with a Common Factor
subject: Mathematics
subtopic: Taking out the highest common factor

scenes.heading: Factorising with a Common Factor
scenes.subheading: Grade 8 Mathematics · Factorisation and equations, part 1
scenes.narration: Welcome to part one of our series on factorisation and equations. In this lesson we learn to factorise by taking out the highest common factor.

scenes.heading: Expanding and factorising
bullets: We take out the highest common factor, the HCF
scenes.narration: You already know how to expand: three times, x plus two, is three x plus six. Factorising goes the other way. We start with three x plus six, and write it as three times, x plus two. To do this, we take out the highest common factor, called the H C F.

scenes.heading: Example 1: Numbers
scenes.narration: Factorise eight x plus twelve. The highest common factor of eight and twelve is four. Divide each term by four: eight x divided by four is two x, and twelve divided by four is three. So the answer is four times, two x plus three.

scenes.heading: Example 2: Variables too
scenes.narration: Factorise five a squared minus fifteen a. The HCF of five and fifteen is five, and both terms have at least one a. So the HCF is five a. Five a squared divided by five a is a. Negative fifteen a divided by five a is negative three. The answer is five a times, a minus three.

scenes.heading: Example 3: Three terms
scenes.narration: Factorise six x cubed, plus nine x squared, minus three x. The HCF is three x. Six x cubed divided by three x is two x squared. Nine x squared divided by three x is three x. And negative three x divided by three x is negative one, not zero. So the answer is three x times, two x squared, plus three x, minus one.

scenes.heading: Example 4: A negative common factor
scenes.narration: Factorise negative four y minus ten. When the first term is negative, take out a negative common factor. The HCF is negative two. Negative four y divided by negative two is two y. Negative ten divided by negative two is positive five. So the answer is negative two times, two y plus five.

scenes.heading: Check by expanding
lines: \text{Same as the question, so it is correct}
scenes.narration: Always check your answer by expanding it. Five a times, a minus three, is five a squared minus fifteen a. That is exactly the expression we started with, so our factorising is correct.

scenes.heading: Tips
bullets: Take out the highest common factor, not just any factor
A term divided by itself leaves 1, not 0
If the first term is negative, take out a negative factor
scenes.narration: Four tips. Take out the highest common factor, not just any common factor. A term divided by itself leaves one, not zero. If the first term is negative, take out a negative factor, and watch the signs change. And always check by expanding.
